headline: Former Canal Dump Becomes Haven for 64% of UK's Black-Necked Grebes
meta_description: A Manchester conservation project turned a 90-year-old dumping ground into a thriving wetland, now home to two-thirds of Britain's breeding black-necked grebes.
summary_short: What was once a dumping ground for canal dredging material has blossomed into a crucial nesting habitat, now sheltering 64% of the UK's black-necked grebes.
body:
A former industrial dumping ground in Manchester has been transformed into a thriving wetland sanctuary, now hosting nearly two-thirds of all breeding black-necked grebes in the United Kingdom. The Woolston Eyes Nature Reserve, sprawling across nearly 1,000 acres between the River Mersey and the Manchester Ship Canal, was originally filled with 41 million cubic meters of material excavated during the canal's construction in the 1890s. After decades of ecological recovery, the site was designated a protected area of special scientific interest in 1986. But the real breakthrough came recently: since 2021, intensive restoration efforts have created ideal nesting conditions, with 35 breeding pairs now recorded by 2025—29 of them on newly restored islands—comprising 64% of the UK's entire population of this rare, ochre-feathered species.

The conservation strategy relies on an elegant partnership between two bird species. Black-headed gulls construct their nests on wetland islands, while black-necked grebes prefer to build nearby, using the gulls as protection. The first arrivals in 2023—just four nesting pairs—produced 15 young, but numbers have since exploded. "It is fantastic to see black-necked grebe numbers increasing at Woolston Eyes thanks to the hard work of staff, volunteers and partners," said Gavin Thomas, an ecologist with the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds, noting that the success demonstrates how effective targeted conservation can be.

The reserve has become a refuge for other vulnerable species too, including willow tits, grasshopper warblers, and pochards. What began as an industrial eyesore nearly a century ago now stands as proof that damaged landscapes can recover when given proper care and commitment.
quick_facts: Woolston Eyes Nature Reserve hosts 35 black-necked grebe pairs as of 2025
Nearly 1,000-acre wetland built from 41 million cubic meters of dredged material
First nesting pairs arrived in 2023, producing 15 young that first season
64% of all UK breeding black-necked grebes now nest at this one site
Site designated protected area in 1986, restored intensively since 2021
